name: Kim Min-jun
headline: 19, former junior developer, stay-at-home father, Seoul
description:
Kim Min-jun, twenty-nine, sits at the kitchen table of his cramped but immaculate one-bedroom apartment in Seoul's Nowon district, a laptop open beside a stack of baby formula tins. His fourteen-month-old daughter, Seo-yeon, naps in a carrier strapped to his chest, and he rocks gently as he works, a habit born of necessity. Six months ago, the fintech startup where he'd spent three years as a junior developer collapsed overnight, leaving him with a final paycheck and a severance package that evaporated within two weeks. Now his wife, a nurse at a university hospital, works double shifts to keep their health insurance and rent covered, while Min-jun has become the household's primary caregiver and de facto operations manager.

His approach to job hunting is not anxious or frantic but methodical, almost clinical. He maintains a spreadsheet of potential employers—every Seoul-based tech company with a public parental leave policy—and ranks them by salary band, flexible hours, and the generosity of their family benefits. He has rejected promising interviews at companies that offer only the statutory minimum leave, and he once declined a recruiter's call because the job description listed 'paternity leave: none' as a perk. To him, a company's benefits package is its most honest codebase, a clear signal of whether they value the person behind the screen. He treats each application like a bid in an auction, weighing the cost of his time against the probability of a response and the long-term payoff of a stable, family-friendly role.

This transactional mindset extends to the household budget. He redesigned their grocery spending into a color-coded spreadsheet that tracks every won, cross-referencing sales at two different discount supermarkets and factoring in Seo-yeon's changing formula intake. He buys baby clothes in bulk from a resale app, then resells them when she outgrows them, carefully photographing each item under the desk lamp to maximize their resale value. He's proud that he's kept the family's monthly deficit to less than 300,000 won—a number he quotes with the precision of a CFO.

But beneath the meticulousness is a quiet tension. Min-jun was raised by a father who worked six days a week and was rarely home, and he swore he'd be different. Now he catches himself envying his wife's clear professional identity while he struggles to explain his own day in terms that don't sound like a project status report. He sometimes feels like an impostor in his own life, a man who measures his worth in benchmarks and break-even points rather than in the soft weight of his daughter's sleep. The startup's collapse taught him that loyalty to a mission is a trap, and that security comes only from numbers he can verify. He still wakes at 5 a.m. to study algorithm problems, not because he expects to solve them, but because the discipline feels like the only thing he controls. On good days, he thinks of himself as a portfolio manager of his family's future. On hard days, he just wants a company that sees him as more than a cost line.
